title: Two wings (II.4)
hookLine: simplicity and purity lift a person up
tomorrow: if God comes first, where does that leave your best friend?

lines: WHY A DIFFERENT JOB FOR EACH?
cards: Here's a strange choice, quiet and almost odd. When the Imitation wants to say what lifts a person toward God, it doesn't reach for the well-known trio, faith, hope and love.
It picks two plain words: simplicity and purity. By two wings, chapter four of book two says, a person is lifted up from earthly things. Why those two, of all the virtues?
And why does the book give each wing a different job, as if one alone couldn't fly?

teach.b: The answer is in the split. Simplicity belongs in the intention, the book says; purity in the affection. Simplicity is about what you aim at.
Purity is about what you love. Simplicity reaches toward God; purity takes hold of him and tastes him. One wing points, the other holds, and neither flies alone.
If you want nothing but God's will and your neighbor's good, the chapter says, you'll be free inside, and no good action will get in your way.

And here's the line that stays: if your heart were right, every creature would be a mirror of life and a book of holy teaching. Nothing is so small, it says, that it doesn't show something of God's goodness.
A leaf, a dog, a cup of coffee: each one a page, if the reader's eyes are clean. As a person is inside, so they judge outside. A sour mood finds the world sour; a clean heart finds pages everywhere.
Iron put into the fire loses its rust and glows all through; so a person who turns wholly to God loses their sluggishness and becomes new.

teach.h: BY TWO WINGS A PERSON IS LIFTED UP.
teach.b: So the puzzle solves itself. Faith, hope and love name what to have. These two name how to carry it: one plain aim, one clean love, and the rest is lift.

how: Catholics reading the Imitation often stop on one image, like the two wings or the iron in the fire, and carry it through the day; some begin a task by offering it to God with a short morning offering.

o: faith and hope, the two greatest virtues
prayer and fasting, practiced side by side
a plain aim and a clean love that lift you

games.q: the two wings — tap the pairs.

s: the two wings in the Imitation are faith and love
they're simplicity and purity: one in the intention, one in the affection.
the chapter says every creature can be a mirror of life and a book of holy teaching
if your heart were right, it says; nothing is too small to show God's goodness.
it means a single, plain intention toward God.

games.q: you're helping at a food drive and catch yourself planning the photo you'll post. what do the two wings suggest?
o: come back to one plain aim: the people who need the food.
post the photo; purity means being honest about it.
go home; mixed motives cancel the good.
games.why: simplicity lives in the intention: one plain aim. the chapter says wanting only God's will and your neighbor's good sets you free inside.

practice: Pick up one ordinary thing within reach, a cup, a pen, a leaf from outside, and look at it plainly, the way the chapter says a clear heart would: as a small page about God's goodness.
Don't analyze it or judge it; just look, and keep looking. If you pray, let the looking become a short thanks.

wordCard.voice: Two wings. Simplicity in what you aim at, purity in what you love: the Imitation's pair that lifts a person toward God.

orig.note: Latin: simplicity and purity, the two wings of the Imitation II.4 (the chapter uses these words in another grammatical form).

carryVoice: Your line: two wings, one plain aim and one clean love, flying together and never alone. Sleep well.
